intro.title: Hangman
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Welcome to the capstone projects. Each one is a complete program built in ten steps, using skills from across the course, and each step adds one piece to the program from the step before. The finished code is yours to keep and change: try it in the sandbox, or copy it onto your own computer and run it there.

The first is **Hangman**, the word-guessing game. The computer picks a secret word and shows a blank for each letter. You guess one letter at a time: right guesses fill in the blanks, and each wrong one costs a life. Find the word before your six lives run out.

```
I'm thinking of a word with 6 letters.
_ _ _ _ _ _   Lives: 6   Wrong: none
Guess a letter: o
Good guess!
_ _ _ _ o _   Lives: 6   Wrong: none
Guess a letter: e
No e in the word
_ _ _ _ o _   Lives: 5   Wrong: e
...
You win! The word was python. Score: 85
```

The game is a handful of small functions: one shows the word with blanks, one checks the player's input, one applies a guess, one sums up the state of play. The guessed letters live in a **set**, because the order doesn't matter and `letter in guessed` is quick. Only the last steps use `input` and `print`; everything before returns values, so each piece can be checked on its own, and the whole game can even be played automatically from a list of guesses.

To play the finished game on your own computer, add `main(["python", "rocket", "planet"])` under a main guard at the bottom of the file. You'll use strings, sets, loops, functions and exceptions from the early sections, `random` from Modules (with a seed, so the checks know which word was picked), and files and JSON for the word list and the high-score table.

intro.title: Budget tracker
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Where does the money go? Build a personal **budget tracker** that records income and spending, sums it up by month and category, warns when a category goes over its limit, and keeps everything in a file between runs.

Each transaction is a small record, a data class with a date, a description, an amount (negative for spending, positive for income) and a category. A `Budget` class holds the transactions and answers questions about them. When it's done, `budget.report("2025-03")` gives:

```
Report for 2025-03
Income 2000.00, spending 417.40, net 1582.60
food      #################### 312.40
fun       ####                 60.00
transport ###                  45.00
Over budget: food: 312.40 of 300.00 (over by 12.40)
```

Dates are kept as ISO text like `2025-03-09`, so `t.date.startswith("2025-03")` picks out a month and sorting by date just works. The budget saves itself as JSON, using `dataclasses.asdict`, and a class method loads it back. It can also export a CSV file, ready for a spreadsheet. The last step puts a command interface on top, the part a user actually types into.

This project brings together classes and data classes, dictionaries for totals, JSON and CSV files, formatting numbers and text, and turning bad input into clear messages.

intro.title: Tic-tac-toe
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Build **tic-tac-toe** (noughts and crosses) and a computer opponent that never loses. You play `X`, the computer plays `O`, and the cells are numbered 1 to 9, left to right and top to bottom:

```
 1 | 2 | 3            X | O |  
---+---+---          ---+---+---
 4 | 5 | 6              | X |  
---+---+---          ---+---+---
 7 | 8 | 9              |   | O
```

The board is a list of nine strings, each `"X"`, `"O"` or `" "`. Cell `n` is `board[n - 1]`, and a three-in-a-row is any of eight lines of positions, written out once as a constant. With that, checking for a winner is a short loop.

The computer player comes in two versions. The first follows simple rules: win if it can, block if it must, otherwise take the centre, then a corner. That's already hard to beat, but not perfect. The second **looks ahead**: it tries every move, then every reply to that move, and so on to the end of the game, assuming both sides play their best. This is the **minimax** idea, and it's naturally recursive: the score of a position is the best (or, on the opponent's turn, the worst) of the scores of the positions one move later.

Looking ahead through every game is a lot of work, and the same positions come up again and again by different routes. So the program remembers each position's score in a dict the first time it works it out. This trick, called **memoisation**, makes the computer's moves instant, fast enough for the last step, which plays every possible game against it to prove it never loses.

You'll use lists and tuples, loops and functions, exceptions for bad moves, recursion from the Functions section, and a dict as a cache.

intro.title: Markdown to HTML
intro.bodyMarkdown:
**Markdown** is the simple text format used for README files, notes and documentation (and for the lessons in this app). You write `**bold**` and `# A heading`, and a converter turns it into **HTML**, the language of web pages. In this project you'll write that converter. Given this Markdown: ``` # Shopping Buy **milk** and *bread* from [the shop](https://example.com). - tea & cake - `coffee` ``` it produces this HTML: ```

Shopping

Buy milk and bread from the shop.

  • tea & cake
  • coffee
``` The work splits into two layers. **Inline** formatting (bold, italics, code and links) happens inside a line, and regular expressions with groups handle it neatly: `re.sub(r"\*\*(.+?)\*\*", r"\1", text)` wraps whatever was between the stars. The `?` makes the match as short as possible, so two bold words in one line stay separate. **Block** structure (headings, paragraphs, lists and code blocks) depends on how lines are grouped, so the converter first splits the text into blocks at blank lines and then decides what each block is. HTML gives `<`, `>` and `&` special meanings, so text has to be **escaped** before it goes into a page: `<` becomes `<`, and so on. Escape first, then add the tags, or the converter would escape its own tags. The finished converter also builds a table of contents and writes a complete web page to a file. You'll use string methods, regular expressions from Data and APIs, functions that build on each other, and files.
intro.sandboxCode: import re text = "Python is **fun** and *easy*. See [docs](https://docs.python.org)." text = re.sub(r"\[([^\]]+)\]\(([^)]+)\)", r'\1', text) text = re.sub(r"\*\*(.+?)\*\*", r"\1", text) text = re.sub(r"\*(.+?)\*", r"\1", text) print(text)

intro.title: Text adventure
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Before games had graphics, they had words. In a **text adventure** you explore a world by typing commands like `go north` and `take lamp`, and the game describes what happens. In this final build you'll write one: an old house with a locked door, a dark library and a treasure in the garden.

```
> look
Hall
A dusty entrance hall.
Exits: east, north
> go east
Kitchen
Pots and pans everywhere.
Exits: west
You see: lamp
> take the lamp
You take the lamp.
```

The world is made of objects. An `Item` is a small data class. A `Room` has a description, exits to other rooms and the items lying in it. The rooms are linked to each other (composition: a room **has** exits that are rooms), so moving is just following a link. A `Player` knows which room they're in and what they carry. A `Game` holds the whole world and turns each typed command into a reply.

Typed commands are messy, so a small **parser** tidies them up first: it lowercases, drops words like "the", and understands short forms, so `n`, `go n` and `walk north` all become `("go", "north")`. Each method returns its reply as text instead of printing it, which is what lets the checks play the game automatically from a list of commands.

The last steps add the things that make it a game: locked doors that need a key, a dark room that needs the lamp, and saving the game to a JSON file and loading it again later. This project uses most of the course: classes, data classes and composition, dicts and lists, string handling, exceptions, and files with JSON.

intro.title: Plan your own project
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The best way to keep learning is to build something of your own. This last project is about **how** to do that: going from an idea to a working program in small, safe steps. The challenges walk through the process on an example, a reading log that tracks the books you're reading, so you can use the same steps for your own idea.

**1. Pick something you'll use.** A tool for your hobby, a game for a friend, a script that saves you ten minutes a week. Then write one sentence saying what it does, and a short list of features. Mark the few you can't do without: that's your first version, the **minimum viable product**. Everything else waits.

```
Reading log: keeps track of the books I'm reading and how far I've got.
Must have:  add a book, record pages read, list my books with progress
Later:      reading goals, stats per year, export to CSV
```

**2. Sketch the data, then the functions.** What does the program remember? Here, books with a title, an author, a page count and how far you are, which makes a good data class. Then list the jobs as small functions, each with a docstring saying what it does. Keep input and output (`input`, `print`, files) at the edges and the logic in the middle, as functions that take values and return values.

**3. Test as you go.** Write a test function for each piece, with a few `assert` lines, often before the code itself. Run them after every change. A test that fails tells you exactly what broke; a program checked only by hand tends to break quietly somewhere else.

**4. Lay out the project** like the Modules section showed: a package for the code, a `tests` folder, a `main.py` that starts it, and a `README.md` saying what it is and how to run it. Put it under version control with git, and commit each time something works.

```
reading_log/
    __init__.py
    books.py        the Book class and the logic
tests/
    test_books.py
main.py             reads commands and calls the logic
README.md
```

**5. Grow it a feature at a time.** Add one feature, test it, commit, repeat. When something is hard, make a smaller version first. When you get stuck, print values, read the error message from the bottom up, and search for it: you've learnt all of these in this course.

Some ideas to start from: a flashcard trainer that saves your scores, a habit or workout log with weekly stats, a recipe book that scales quantities, a budget that reads your bank's CSV export, a quiz or word game for a friend, a tool that renames and sorts your photos by date, a script that checks a website's prices from its API, or a small text game. Where next? Flask or Django for websites, pandas and matplotlib for data, pygame for games, and pytest for testing bigger projects.

tests.assertion: Book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", 412, 412).finished is True and Book("Emma", "Jane Austen", 474, 10).finished is False

challenges.title: Easy: A documented function
challenges.promptMarkdown: Define `progress(pages_read: int, pages: int) -> int` with a docstring, returning how far through a book you are as a whole percentage (rounded down), never more than 100, and 0 when `pages` is 0 or less.
challenges.hint: `min(100, pages_read * 100 // pages)`, after checking `pages`.

tests.label: Documented
tests.assertion: bool(progress.__doc__) and progress.__annotations__ == {"pages_read": int, "pages": int, "return": int}

challenges.title: Easy: Write the tests
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `test_progress()`, a test function with `assert` lines checking `progress` at least for: the start (0 pages read), part way, past the end, and a book with 0 pages.
challenges.hint: One `assert progress(...) == ...` for each case. The checks swap in broken versions of `progress` to see whether your test catches them.

tests.label: Catches no limit at 100
tests.assertion: _catches(test_progress, "progress", lambda r, p: r * 100 // p if p > 0 else 0)

tests.label: Catches a crash on 0 pages
tests.assertion: _catches_any(test_progress, "progress", lambda r, p: min(100, r * 100 // p))

tests.label: Catches rounding up
tests.assertion: _catches(test_progress, "progress", lambda r, p: min(100, -(-r * 100 // p)) if p > 0 else 0)

challenges.title: Medium: The first feature
challenges.promptMarkdown: Define `add_book(log, title, author, pages)` that adds a `Book` to the list `log` and returns it, trimming the title and author. Raise `ValueError` with `A book needs a title and an author`, `Pages must be more than 0`, or `<title> is already in your log` (ignoring case).
challenges.hint: Check everything before appending.

tests.label: Refused
tests.assertion: (lambda log: (add_book(log, "Dune", "F", 1), [_error(add_book, log, *a) for a in (("", "X", 5), ("Emma", "Jane Austen", 0), ("DUNE", "F", 9))])[1])([]) == ["ValueError: A book needs a title and an author", "ValueError: Pages must be more than 0", "ValueError: DUNE is already in your log"]

challenges.title: Medium: Read commands
challenges.promptMarkdown: Define `parse_command(text)` that splits a command with `shlex.split`, so quoted words stay together, and returns `(command, arguments)` with the command lowercased. Raise `ValueError("Type a command")` for an empty one and `ValueError("Check your quotes")` when `shlex` can't split it.
challenges.hint: `shlex.split` raises `ValueError` for an unclosed quote: catch it and raise your own message.

tests.label: Quotes
tests.assertion: parse_command('ADD "The Hobbit" "J. R. R. Tolkien" 310') == ("add", ["The Hobbit", "J. R. R. Tolkien", "310"])

tests.label: Errors
tests.assertion: [_error(parse_command, t) for t in ("   ", 'add "Dune')] == ["ValueError: Type a command", "ValueError: Check your quotes"]

challenges.title: Medium: Save your work

tests.assertion: (lambda log: (save_log(log, "books.json"), load_log("books.json") == log)[1])([Book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", 412, 50), Book("Emma", "Jane Austen", 474)])

questions.prompt: What is a minimum viable product?

choices.label: The smallest program Python can run
The few must-have features that make a first useful version

questions.explanation: An MVP is the smallest version that is actually useful; the rest comes after.

questions.prompt: Where should `input`, `print` and file handling go?

choices.label: At the edges, with the logic in functions that take and return values

questions.explanation: Keeping input and output at the edges leaves the core logic easy to test.

questions.prompt: Why write tests as you go?

choices.label: A failing test tells you exactly what broke, straight after a change

questions.explanation: Tests run straight after each change show exactly what broke.

questions.prompt: What does `shlex.split('add "The Hobbit" 310')` give?
questions.explanation: `shlex.split` respects quotes, so a title with spaces stays one argument.

questions.prompt: Where do a project's test files usually go?

choices.label: Nowhere: tests are run by hand

questions.explanation: Projects usually keep their test files together in a `tests/` folder.

questions.prompt: How should a project grow after its first version?

choices.label: One feature at a time: add, test, commit, repeat

questions.explanation: Small, tested steps keep the project working all the time.

questions.prompt: How does pytest find tests?

choices.label: By looking for functions whose names start with `test_`
It needs a list of them

questions.explanation: pytest collects functions named `test_...` from test files.

questions.prompt: When does `main` save the log?
questions.explanation: Saving only after a command succeeds means a failed command never changes the saved data.
